en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Puzzles, Section One: The Power of Psychic Faculties (Iddhibalavagga)
4. The Question on the Earthquake “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, there are these eight causes, eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake.’”
This is an exhaustive statement; this is a complete statement; this is a non-figurative statement. There is no other ninth cause for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Venerable Nāgasena, if there were another ninth cause for the manifestation of a great earthquake, the Blessed One would have mentioned that cause as well.
But since, venerable Nāgasena, there is no other ninth cause for the manifestation of a great earthquake, [this is indeed the case].
Therefore, this ninth cause for the manifestation of a great earthquake, which was not mentioned by the Blessed One— namely,
that the great earth shook seven times while King Vessantara was bestowing his great gift—
is now seen. If, venerable Nāgasena, there are only eight causes and eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake, [how is this to be accounted for?]
Therefore, the statement that "when the great gift was being given by King Vessantara, the great earth shook seven times" is false.

If it were true that the great earth shook seven times when the great gift was being given by King Vessantara, then the statement that "there are eight causes and eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake" would also be false.

“This too is a double-edged question, subtle, difficult to unravel, both darkening and profound; it has come to you, and it cannot be answered by anyone else of limited wisdom other than one as intelligent as you.
“Indeed, Great King, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, there are these eight causes, eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake.’”

When King Vessantara was bestowing the great gift, the great earth shook seven times; yet that was not counted among the eight causes because it was unseasonable, occurring at an improper time, and free from the eight [standard] causes.

Great King, just as in the world only three kinds of clouds are reckoned—the rain-cloud, the winter-cloud, and the monsoon-cloud—if another cloud should rain apart from those, it is not reckoned among the recognized types of clouds, but is designated simply as an "unseasonable cloud."

"In the same way, Great King, when King Vessantara was bestowing his great gift, as for the fact that the great earth shook seven times—this was not a timely occurrence arising from a specific cause, but was free from the eight causes; it is not counted among those eight causes.
Or again, Great King, just as five hundred rivers flow from the Himavat mountains, yet of those five hundred rivers, only ten are counted in the reckoning of rivers."
For example—the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, Mahī, Sindhu, Sarassatī, Vetravatī, Vītansā, and Candabhāgā; all other rivers remain uncounted in the enumeration of rivers.
For what reason?
Those rivers do not have constant waters.
In the same way, Great King, when King Vessantara was giving the great gift, that the great earth shook seven times was not caused by the eight causes;
it was untimely, occurring at an unexpected moment, and free from the eight causes—it is not reckoned among those eight causes.
Or again, great king, suppose a king has a hundred, two hundred, or even three hundred ministers; yet among them, only six persons are counted in the reckoning of ministers.
Namely: the commander-in-chief, the chaplain, the keeper of the dice, the treasurer, the umbrella-bearer, and the sword-bearer.
These alone are counted by the calculation of ministers.
For what reason?
Because they are endowed with the qualities of a king; the rest are not counted, as all of them are merely reckoned as "ministers."

“In the same way, Great King, when King Vessantara was giving his great gift, that the great earth shook seven times—this was not a timely occurrence arising from a specific cause, but was free from the eight causes; it is not reckoned among those eight causes.

Now, Great King, is there heard nowadays in the teaching of the Conqueror the report of deeds to be experienced as happiness in this very life performed by those whose fame has spread among gods and men?”

“Yes, venerable sir, it is heard nowadays that there are seven persons who have performed meritorious deeds within the Dispensation of the Conqueror, whose karma is to be experienced as happiness in this very life, and whose fame has spread among gods and humans.
“And who are they, Great King?
“Venerable sir, they are Sumana the garland-maker, the Brahmin Ekasāṭaka, Puṇṇa the laborer, and Mallikā...”
“Queen Mallikā, Queen Gopālamātā, the female lay follower Suppiyā, and the maidservant Puṇṇā— these seven beings experienced happiness in this very life,
and their fame has spread among gods and humans.
“Are there others as well who, it is heard, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in their human bodies alone in the past?”
“Yes, venerable sir, they are heard.
“But who are they, Great King?
“Guttila the musician, King Sādhīna, King Nimi, and King Mandhātā—these four persons are heard to have gone to the realm of the Thirty-three with their very human bodies.”
“Is it heard that good and evil deeds endure even for a very long time?
But have you ever heard, Great King, whether in the past or in the present, that when a gift was being given by someone named so-and-so, the great earth shook once, twice, or three times?
“No indeed, Bhante.”
“Great King, I possess scriptural tradition, realization, mastery, learning, the strength of training, a desire to hear, inquiry, and attendance upon teachers;
yet even by me has it never been heard before that ‘while such-and-such a gift was being given,
the great earth shook once, twice, or thrice,’ with the exception of the noble gift of Vessantara, the bull among kings.”
“Great King, between the Blessed One Kassapa and the Blessed One Śākyamuni,
more than millions of years have passed beyond the reach of calculation; even during that time,
I have no recollection of hearing it said that ‘while a gift was being given by such-and-such a person, the great earth shook once, twice, or thrice.’”
"No, Great King, it is not by such mere vigor or such mere exertion that the great earth shakes.
Rather, Great King, being laden with the burden of virtues—being laden with the burden of virtues consisting of all acts of purity—the great earth, unable to sustain it, trembles, shakes, and quakes.
Just as, Great King, when a cart is overloaded with an excessive burden, its hubs and rims burst and its axle breaks."
In the same way, Great King, the great earth, unable to bear the burden of the weight of all those acts of purification and virtuous deeds, trembles, shakes, and quakes.
Or again, Great King, just as the sky, when covered by the force of wind and water and filled with a heavy mass of water, roars, resounds, and gurgles due to being struck by a violent wind;
even so, Great King, the great earth, unable to bear the burden of the vast and overflowing weight of King Vessantara’s power of giving, trembles, shakes, and quakes.
For indeed, Great King, King Vessantara’s mind does not proceed by way of lust,

nor does it proceed by way of hatred, nor does it proceed by way of delusion, nor does it proceed by way of conceit, nor does it proceed by way of wrong view, nor does it proceed by way of the defilements,
nor does it proceed by way of discursive thought, nor does it proceed by way of discontent; rather, it proceeds by way of generosity.
His mind was constantly and continuously fixed upon giving, thinking: "How might future supplicants come to me, and having arrived, how might they be satisfied by receiving whatever they desire?

Great King, the mind of King Vessantara was constantly and continuously fixed upon ten things: self-control, equanimity, patience, restraint, self-restraint, regulation, non-anger, non-violence, truthfulness, and purity.
Great King, King Vessantara has abandoned the search for sensual pleasures and stilled the search for existence; he has applied himself with zeal only to the search for the holy life.
Great King, King Vessantara has abandoned self-protection and applied himself with zeal to the protection of all beings, such that his mind frequently dwells on this:
"How may these beings be harmonious, free from disease, possessed of wealth, and long-lived?"

And while giving that gift, great king, King Vessantara did not give for the sake of attaining a fortunate rebirth; he did not give for the sake of wealth; he did not give for the sake of a return gift;
he did not give for the sake of flattery; he did not give for the sake of long life;
he did not give for the sake of beauty; he did not give for the sake of pleasure; he did not give for the sake of strength; he did not give for the sake of fame; he did not give for the sake of sons.

He did not give them for the sake of his daughter; rather, it was for the sake of omniscient knowledge, for the purpose of the jewel of omniscience, that he gave such incomparable, vast, and unsurpassed supreme gifts. And having attained omniscience, he uttered this verse:
“Jāli, Kaṇhājinā, and my daughter...”
‘Even while renouncing Maddīdevī,
who was devoted to me, I did not worry,
solely for the sake of awakening.’”

"Vessantara, O Great King, was a king who conquered anger with non-anger, conquered the wicked with goodness, conquered the miserly with generosity, conquered the speaker of falsehoods with truth, and conquered all that is unwholesome with what is wholesome.

As he was thus giving, following the Dhamma and headed by the Dhamma, through the great power, vast expansion, and abundance of his energy resulting from the flow of his generosity, the great winds below were stirred;
they blew slowly, gently, and repeatedly, becoming turbulent, bowing down."
They rise and fall; trees with severed leaves fall down; clouds rush together in clusters across the sky;
winds gathered from dust become violent; winds press upon the sky and blow, suddenly roaring with a tumultuous sound;
a great and terrifying noise issues forth; when those winds are agitated, the water trembles very slowly, and within that water...
When it moves, the fish and turtles are agitated; twin upon twin waves arise; aquatic beings tremble;
the water ripples flow in pairs; the roar of the waves resounds; fierce bubbles emerge; garlands of foam form;
the great ocean overflows; the water rushes toward every direction and intermediate direction, with currents flowing both upward and backward.
Streams of water flow forth; the asuras, garuḷas, nāgas, and yakkhas tremble and are terrified, wondering, "What now?
How is it that the ocean is being overturned? With hearts filled with fear, they seek a path to flee.
When the streams of water are agitated and churned, the great earth, together with its mountains and oceans, quakes; Mount Sineru, with its peaks, crags, and summits, turns around, bending low.
The snakes, mongooses, cats, jackals, pigs, deer, and birds become distressed;
the lesser *yakkhas* weep, while the more powerful *yakkhas* laugh as the great earth trembles.
Great King, it is just as when a large cauldron is placed over a fire, filled with water and heaped with rice from below.
When a fire is burning, first it heats the pot; the heated pot heats the water;
the heated water heats the rice; the heated rice bubbles up and subsides, becomes covered with froth, and a garland of foam rises up.
In the same way, Great King, King Vessantara gave that which is difficult to give in the world.
As he was giving that which is so difficult to give, because of the natural outflow of that gift, the great winds below were unable to hold their ground and became turbulent.
When the great winds became turbulent, the water shook; when the water shook, the great earth shook. Thus, at that time, the great winds—
The water and the great earth—these three became as if of one mind through the overflow of that great gift and its vast power and energy.
Great King, there is no such majesty of another’s giving as the majesty of King Vessantara’s great giving.
Great King, it is just as various kinds of jewels are found upon the earth.
That is to say:

the indanīla, the mahānīla, the jotirasa, the beryl, the umā-flower, the sirīsa-flower, the manohara, the sun-loved, the moon-loved, the diamond, the firefly-gem, the phussa-rāga, the ruby, and the musāragalva; surpassing all these—
The wheel-turning monarch’s gem is declared supreme; for, great king, the wheel-turning monarch’s gem illuminates an area for a league all around.

Even so, great king, whatever gift exists on earth—even including the peerless gift that is supreme—all of that is surpassed, and the Great Gift of King Vessantara is declared supreme. Of King Vessantara, great king...
“When the King’s great almsgiving was being bestowed, the great earth shook seven times.
“It is wonderful, venerable Nāgasena, regarding the Buddhas;

it is marvelous, venerable Nāgasena, regarding the Buddhas, that the Tathāgata, while still a Bodhisatta, was thus peerless in the world, possessing such conduct, such thoughts, such resolve, and such intention.”
"Venerable Nāgasena, the exertion of the Bodhisattvas has been demonstrated, and the perfections of the Conquerors have been further illuminated;
even while practicing the conduct, the preeminence of the Tathāgata in the world with its devas has been shown.
Well done, venerable Nāgasena! The teaching of the Conqueror has been praised, the perfection of the Conqueror has been made radiant, and the heretics have been refuted."
“The knot of debate has been untied; the jar of slander against others has been shattered; the profound question has been made clear; the thicket has been cleared of its density;

the vehicle for the sons of the Conqueror has been rightly obtained. It is even so, O most excellent chief of assemblies; we accept it as such. Thus ends the fourth discourse, “The Question on the Earthquake.”
